papers.title: Hypoxia Triggers BNIP3/BNIP3L-Associated Mitophagy in HT22 Immortalized Hippocampal Neurons: A Temporal Descriptive Study.
papers.summary: This study looks at how hippocampal neurons (using the HT22 cell line) respond to low-oxygen conditions by activating mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria. The researchers focused on two specific proteins, BNIP3 and BNIP3L, which act as receptors that tag mitochondria for degradation during hypoxia. By tracking changes over time, they describe how this mitophagy pathway unfolds as a temporal sequence of events following oxygen deprivation.
papers.why: Understanding the molecular timeline of BNIP3/BNIP3L-mediated mitophagy in hippocampal neurons provides a mechanistic foundation relevant to the PhD project's focus on neuronal mitophagy, which could inform how spatial transcriptomic or metabolomic signatures of mitophagy might be identified in brain tissue.
papers.figure: A time-course figure showing BNIP3/BNIP3L expression levels alongside mitophagy markers (e.g., LC3, mitochondrial mass) across different hypoxia durations.

papers.title: Sephin1 directly targets PHB2 to activate PINK1-PRKN-dependent mitophagy and alleviate α-synuclein neurotoxicity in Parkinson's disease models.
papers.summary: This paper investigates a drug called Sephin1 and finds that it binds directly to a protein called PHB2, which is involved in mitochondrial quality control. This interaction triggers PINK1-PRKN-dependent mitophagy, a process where damaged mitochondria are selectively cleared from cells. In models of Parkinson's disease, boosting this mitophagy pathway with Sephin1 reduced the toxic effects of α-synuclein, a protein central to Parkinson's pathology.
papers.why: This work provides direct mechanistic and pharmacological evidence for enhancing PINK1-PRKN-dependent mitophagy in neurons, offering both a molecular target (PHB2) and a candidate compound relevant to studying mitophagy dysregulation in neurodegeneration.
papers.figure: Figure showing Sephin1-PHB2 binding assay alongside mitophagy flux markers (e.g., mitochondrial PINK1/PRKN recruitment and mitophagy reporter assays) in neuronal models.

papers.title: 1,2-Dichloroethane Induces Neuronal Apoptosis Through AMPK-mTOR-ULK1 Pathway Activation and Autophagic Flux Impairment.
papers.summary: This study looks at how the industrial chemical 1,2-dichloroethane damages neurons by causing them to undergo apoptosis (programmed cell death). The researchers found that the toxin activates a cellular energy-sensing pathway called AMPK-mTOR-ULK1, which normally triggers autophagy (the cell's recycling process). However, instead of properly clearing cellular waste, this activation actually disrupts the autophagic flux, meaning autophagosomes form but aren't properly cleared, contributing to neuronal death.
papers.why: This paper provides direct mechanistic insight into how autophagic flux impairment and dysregulation of the AMPK-mTOR-ULK1 pathway contribute to neuronal death, offering a toxin-induced model that could inform interpretation of autophagy/mitophagy disruptions studied in the PhD project's neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Mitochondria Take Up and Dispose of Cytosolic Protein Aggregates
papers.summary: This paper describes a newly discovered mechanism in which mitochondria directly internalize misfolded or aggregated proteins from the cytosol. Once inside, these aggregates are degraded using the mitochondria's own proteolytic machinery, effectively acting as a disposal pathway distinct from classical autophagy. This suggests mitochondria play an active, previously underappreciated role in cellular protein quality control.
papers.why: This finding is highly relevant because it reveals an alternative, mitochondria-based route for clearing misfolded proteins that could intersect with or compensate for mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, potentially reshaping how protein aggregate clearance is interpreted in brain tissue.
papers.figure: Figure showing time-course imaging/electron microscopy of cytosolic aggregate uptake into mitochondria and subsequent degradation.

papers.title: Targeting neuronal injury with intranasal Arc-engineered exosomes rescues cognitive deficits in Alzheimer's disease via the mTOR-autophagy pathway.
papers.summary: This study engineers exosomes to carry the Arc protein and delivers them through the nose to treat Alzheimer's disease in an animal model. The Arc-exosomes appear to reduce neuronal damage and improve memory/cognitive function. The mechanism involves regulating the mTOR-autophagy pathway, which controls how cells clear damaged components.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly links autophagy pathway modulation to neuronal injury and cognitive rescue in a neurodegenerative disease, offering a therapeutic angle that complements mechanistic mitophagy/autophagy research in neurons.
papers.figure: A figure showing autophagy markers (e.g., LC3, p62) and mTOR pathway activity in neurons after Arc-exosome treatment, ideally paired with cognitive/behavioral outcome measures.

papers.title: Mitochondria-ER contact sites in neurological disorders.
papers.summary: This paper reviews mitochondria-ER contact sites (MERCS), specialized membrane junctions where mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum physically interact to exchange calcium, lipids, and signals. It discusses how disruption of these contact sites is implicated in various neurological disorders, likely through effects on mitochondrial function, calcium homeostasis, and cellular stress responses. The abstract suggests a broad overview connecting MERCS biology to disease mechanisms in the nervous system.
papers.why: MERCS regulate mitochondrial quality control and calcium signaling that directly influence mitophagy initiation and mitochondrial health in neurons, making this relevant background for understanding neuronal autophagy dysfunction.

papers.title: Mitochondrial Quality Control Imbalance in the Heterogeneity of Parkinson's Disease: From Selective Vulnerability to Stratified Transformation.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how imbalances in mitochondrial quality control—processes like mitophagy, fission/fusion, and biogenesis—contribute to the heterogeneity seen among Parkinson's disease patients. It proposes that different neuron populations show selective vulnerability to mitochondrial dysfunction, which may explain why disease presentation and progression vary so much between individuals. The authors suggest that understanding this heterogeneity could enable stratified treatment approaches tailored to specific patient subgroups based on their underlying mitochondrial quality control defects.
papers.why: This directly informs the mechanistic backbone of the PhD project, since mitophagy imbalance driving selective neuronal vulnerability is central to understanding why specific interneuron populations may be differentially affected in neurodegeneration.
papers.figure: A figure mapping mitochondrial quality control pathway alterations onto specific vulnerable neuron subtypes or brain regions would be most informative for linking mechanism to selective vulnerability.
